people.name: Carlos Mariani
body: In January 1991, a community organizer from St. Paul took his seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives. Carlos Mariani would hold it for more than three decades, until January 2023. When he announced his retirement he recalled, "For eight years I was the only Latino in our state Legislature."

Mariani's story starts in Chicago. He grew up on the city's West Side, one of four sons of Carlos and Carmen Mariani, Puerto Rican parents who worked hard to make a living there. One fact helps here: people born in Puerto Rico are U.S. citizens by birth. Starting in the mid-twentieth century, large numbers moved from the island to cities such as New York and Chicago as citizens, not as immigrants in the legal sense.

Mariani came to Minnesota on a partial scholarship to Macalester College, where he earned a history degree. He spent a year at the University of Minnesota law school but did not go back. He took a job as a paralegal at St. Paul's Neighborhood Justice Center, which provided criminal defense for low-income people of color, and then organized in the Latino community for the Minnesota Council of Churches.

He won his House seat in 1990. Alongside his legislative work he led the Minnesota Minority Education Partnership, a nonprofit working with students, parents, teachers and public officials to raise achievement among students of color. In the Legislature he chaired the House Education Policy committee and, in his final term, the Public Safety and Criminal Justice Reform Finance and Policy committee. When he retired, he named immigration law reform, racial integration of public schools, preservation of heritage languages and the Minnesota Police Accountability Act among the work he was proudest of.
keyFacts: 1957: Born July 13.
Raised on Chicago's West Side by Puerto Rican parents; graduated from Macalester College with a history degree.
1990: Elected; served in the Minnesota House for District 65B (St. Paul) from January 1991 to January 2023.
Executive director of the Minnesota Minority Education Partnership; chaired the House Education Policy committee.
2022: Chose not to run for re-election.
people.connectToWork: When a form or intake script asks where someone is from or about their immigration status, what would it assume about a person who is a U.S. citizen by birth and came here through Chicago?

people.name: Ricardo Levins Morales
body: In a studio on Minnehaha Avenue in south Minneapolis, posters, buttons and organizing zines carry bold images and short lessons out into the world. This is the studio of Ricardo Levins Morales. The McKnight Foundation says he creates art as a form of medicine, to support healing from and resistance to oppression.

Levins Morales was born in Puerto Rico into the island's anti-colonial movement. Some context helps here. Puerto Rico has been a U.S. territory since 1898, and debates over its political status have shaped generations of activism. In 1967 his family moved to Chicago. There, as a teenager, he was drawn into activism, including support work for the Black Panthers and the Young Lords, a Puerto Rican organizing group. He left high school early and worked in a range of industries, combining art with organizing.

He moved to Minnesota in 1976 and was a founding member of the Northland Poster Collective, which from 1979 to 2009 made art alongside unions and movements for labor, farmer, environmental and racial justice. He now runs RLM Art Studio and leads workshops on creative organizing and sustainable activism. With Line Break Media he made the short video The Soil Is More Important than the Seeds, which argues that movements succeed when the ground they grow in is cared for.
In 2024 the McKnight Foundation named him its Distinguished Artist. The honor, given each year since 1998 with a $100,000 award, recognizes artists who have made lasting contributions to Minnesota.
keyFacts: Born in Puerto Rico; family moved to Chicago in 1967.
1976: Moved to Minnesota.
1979–2009: Northland Poster Collective, which he helped found.
Runs RLM Art Studio in south Minneapolis.
2024: McKnight Foundation Distinguished Artist.
people.connectToWork: Before your team starts a new effort with people affected by a system, what would you do first to care for the ground it grows in, such as trust, time and pay?

people.name: José Antonio Zayas Cabán
body: Few people lead a streets advocacy group and also earn Grammy nominations as a saxophonist. José Antonio Zayas Cabán does both. He was born and raised in Mayagüez, on Puerto Rico's west coast, and now lives in Minneapolis.

As a musician he is a multi-Grammy-nominated saxophonist and a McKnight Fellow. He teaches saxophone at St. Joseph's School of Music and co-founded the chamber trio {trés}. With them he developed Pedacito de Tierra, a performance about the Puerto Rican community in Minnesota that combines music, storytelling and oral histories. The Minnesota Historical Society announced its free world premiere for January 15, 2026, at the Minnesota History Center, with music by Angélica Negrón, Miguel Zenón as guest, and a companion exhibit with artwork by Ricardo Levins Morales.
He also appeared on the Minnesota Historical Society podcast Minnesota Unraveled and wrote a related storymap on the Puerto Rican diaspora in the Twin Cities.

As an advocate he is executive director of Our Streets, a Minneapolis organization focused on how streets are designed and who they serve. He develops reparative justice campaigns across the Twin Cities, including work on how highways and planning decisions damaged neighborhoods of color. Examples are Bring Back 6th! in North Minneapolis and the Twin Cities Boulevard proposal for the I-94 corridor. He was a 2022–2023 Community Fellow with the Mapping Prejudice Project. He received a 2021 McKnight Artist Fellowship for albums about present-day social issues and the relationship between Puerto Rico and the United States, and he is a 2026 Bush Fellow.
keyFacts: Born and raised in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico; lives in Minneapolis.
Multi-Grammy-nominated saxophonist; co-founder of the trio {trés}.
Executive director of Our Streets, as of October 2026.
2021: McKnight Artist Fellowship.
2026: Bush Fellow.
January 15, 2026: Announced date for the world premiere of Pedacito de Tierra.

people.name: Tearra Oso
body: In St. Paul community arts centers, Tearra Oso leads circles of people drumming the rhythms of bomba, an Afro-Boricua (Afro-Puerto Rican) practice of drumming, song and dance. As Oso describes it, bomba was created by enslaved West African people on the sugar cane plantations of Puerto Rico in the 1500s.
Oso grew up in St. Paul and learned bomba there. That detail matters. Afro-Puerto Rican tradition has been taught and passed down in Minnesota itself.

She created a sound she calls BombaPop, which joins bomba with pop, funk, R&B and hip-hop, sung in English and Spanish. She has said that being a former classmate of Philando Castile, along with the 2020 murder of George Floyd, moved her to make an album built on bomba rhythms. Before that she worked internationally as a model and appeared in film and television, including Extant and Live by Night. Her debut album, PREZ (2022), was featured by The Current, which described its blend of bomba percussion, funky guitar and layered vocals. The Minnesota Historical Society reports that the Star Tribune named it one of Minnesota's top 10 albums of 2022. She also released the EPs Art Projects, Vol. 1 (2012) and Vol. 2 (2020) and received a 2021 Cedar Commission.

Oso also uses bomba for healing, leading drumming sessions at St. Paul's Black Youth Healing Arts Center and Indigenous Roots Cultural Arts Center. The Minnesota Historical Society describes her as a performer, healer and "culture protector."
keyFacts: Grew up in St. Paul, where she learned Afro-Boricua bomba.
2012 and 2020: Released the EPs Art Projects, Vol. 1 and Vol. 2.
2021: Received a Cedar Commission.
2022: Released her debut album, PREZ.
Leads bomba drumming sessions at the Black Youth Healing Arts Center and Indigenous Roots Cultural Arts Center.

people.name: Arturo Alfonso Schomburg
body: In 1926 the New York Public Library bought a private collection of books, manuscripts and prints documenting the history of people of African descent, using a $10,000 grant from the Carnegie Corporation. The collection, more than four thousand items by the American Academy of Arts and Sciences' account, went to the library's 135th Street branch in Harlem. It became the core of what is now the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture. The man who built it was born in Puerto Rico.

Arturo Alfonso Schomburg was born on January 24, 1874, in San Juan, and arrived in New York City on April 17, 1891. He joined the movement for independence from Spain, helping found the political club Las Dos Antillas and serving as its secretary from 1892 to 1896.

Schomburg was Afro-Puerto Rican. He set out to disprove the claim, common in his era, that Black people had no history, gathering evidence of African and Afro-diasporic achievement from across the Americas and Europe. In 1911 he helped organize the Negro Society for Historical Research, and in the 1920s he served as president of the American Negro Academy. The American Historical Association and the New York Public Library give different end years for that post, 1928 and 1929.

After the 1926 sale he continued to shape the collection. In 1932 he became curator of the Schomburg Collection of Negro Literature and Art at the 135th Street branch, and he held the post until his death on June 10, 1938.
keyFacts: 1874: Born January 24 in San Juan, Puerto Rico.
1891: Arrived in New York on April 17.
1892–1896: Secretary of Las Dos Antillas.
1911: Helped organize the Negro Society for Historical Research.
1926: The New York Public Library acquired his collection with a $10,000 Carnegie Corporation grant.
1932–1938: Curator of the collection until his death on June 10, 1938.

people.name: Antonia Pantoja
body: During World War II, a young woman from San Juan worked as a welder in a New York factory making children's lamps, and helped organize her coworkers into a union. That was Antonia Pantoja. She went on to found institutions that serve Puerto Rican and Latino young people to this day.
Pantoja arrived in New York in 1944. In the postwar decades, large numbers of Puerto Ricans moved to New York as U.S. citizens, mostly for factory and service jobs. She trained as a social worker.

In 1957 she founded the Hispanic American Youth Association, which later became the National Puerto Rican Forum. In 1961 she founded ASPIRA, a nonprofit that promotes education and leadership among Puerto Rican and other Latino youth, and which still operates. Its name comes from the Spanish word for "aspire." In 1972 ASPIRA sued the New York City Board of Education over instruction for Spanish-speaking students, a case that helped lead to landmark bilingual education legislation. In 1970 she created the Puerto Rican Research and Resource Center in Washington, D.C., work that led to the founding of Boricua College in the early 1970s.
In 1996 President Bill Clinton awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The Museum of the City of New York describes her as the first Latina to receive it. She died in 2002.
keyFacts: 1922: Born September 13 in San Juan, by the Museum of the City of New York's account. Brooklyn College's Latinas in History page gives 1921.
1944: Arrived in New York.
1957: Founded the Hispanic American Youth Association, later the National Puerto Rican Forum.
1961: Founded ASPIRA.
1970: Created a research center in Washington, D.C., that led to Boricua College.
1996: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
2002: Died.

people.name: Pura Belpré
body: In May 1921, the New York Public Library's 135th Street branch in Harlem hired a young woman from Cidra, Puerto Rico, as its Spanish-speaking assistant. Pura Belpré became the library system's first Puerto Rican librarian. She went on to change how American libraries serve Spanish-speaking children.
Belpré started Spanish-language and bilingual story programs, using handmade puppets and oral storytelling to bring island folklore to children in both languages.

She also wrote those stories down. In 1932 Frederick Warne published her Pérez and Martina, about a cockroach and a mouse, described as the first Puerto Rican folktale published in the United States. More books followed.

Belpré returned to the library in 1960 as a Spanish children's specialist. In 1968 the librarian Augusta Baker brought her into the South Bronx Library Project, an outreach program for low-income, Spanish-speaking neighborhoods. On June 30, 1982, the New York Public Library honored her. She died in her sleep the next day.

In 1996 the American Library Association and REFORMA, the national association promoting library services to Latinos, created the Pura Belpré Award for Latino writers and illustrators of children's books. Sources disagree on the year she was born, giving dates from 1899 to 1903.
keyFacts: Born in Cidra, Puerto Rico; birth year disputed.
1921: Hired in May at the New York Public Library's 135th Street branch, the system's first Puerto Rican librarian.
1932: Pérez and Martina published.
1968: Joined the South Bronx Library Project.
1982: Died July 1.
1996: American Library Association and REFORMA established the Pura Belpré Award.

people.name: Helen Rodríguez Trías
body: In 1970 Dr. Helen Rodríguez Trías became head of pediatrics at Lincoln Hospital in the South Bronx, which the National Park Service says served mostly Black and Latino patients. She pushed to give every hospital worker, not only the doctors, a voice in decisions about running the hospital and caring for patients.

Rodríguez Trías was born in New York in 1929, spent her early childhood in Puerto Rico and came back to New York at age 10. School administrators placed her in less advanced classes despite her good grades. She later studied at the University of Puerto Rico and earned her medical degree there in 1960. During her residency she founded Puerto Rico's first newborn care center, which, by the National Library of Medicine's account, cut the hospital's newborn death rate by half within three years.

Her best-known work was against sterilization abuse. Through the mid-twentieth century, large numbers of women in Puerto Rico and poor women of color on the mainland were sterilized, often without real informed consent. She helped found the Committee to End Sterilization Abuse in 1970 and the Committee for Abortion Rights and Against Sterilization Abuse in 1979. That year she testified in support of federal sterilization guidelines she had helped draft. They require written consent, in a language the patient understands, and a waiting period.

In the 1980s she was medical director of the New York State Department of Health AIDS Institute, working on behalf of women with HIV. In 1993 she became the first Latina elected president of the American Public Health Association. In January 2001 she received the Presidential Citizens Medal. She died in December 2001.
keyFacts: 1929: Born in New York; spent her early years in Puerto Rico.
1960: M.D., University of Puerto Rico.
1970: Became head of pediatrics at Lincoln Hospital, South Bronx.
1979: Testified for federal sterilization consent guidelines she helped draft.
1993: First Latina president of the American Public Health Association.
2001: Presidential Citizens Medal; died December 27.
people.connectToWork: If someone is cautious about a consent form or a medical referral, how would you ask what has shaped that caution? Is your consent process truly in a language the person understands?

people.name: Rita Moreno
body: At the 1962 Academy Awards, Rita Moreno won Best Supporting Actress for playing Anita in West Side Story. She became the first Latina to win an Oscar.

Moreno was born Rosita Dolores Alverio Marcano on December 11, 1931, in Humacao, Puerto Rico. At age 5 she moved to New York City with her mother. She made her Broadway debut at 13 in Skydrift (1945). In 1950 she signed with MGM, and she played Tuptim in The King and I (1956) before West Side Story.

She then built one of the widest-ranging careers in American entertainment. She won a Grammy in 1972 for The Electric Company Album, tied to the children's TV show that taught reading, a Tony in 1975 for The Ritz and an Emmy in 1977 for The Muppet Show, becoming the first Latina to win all four. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2004, the National Medal of Arts in 2009, a Kennedy Center Honor in 2015 and a Peabody Career Achievement Award in 2019.

In 2021, at almost 90, she returned to West Side Story in Steven Spielberg's remake, playing the new role of Valentina. As of October 2026 she is still making public appearances, including a conversation at Lehman College in New York.
keyFacts: 1931: Born December 11 in Humacao, Puerto Rico.
1936: Moved to New York.
1962: Academy Award for West Side Story, the first Latina Oscar winner.
Grammy (1972), Tony (1975), Emmy (1977).
2004: Presidential Medal of Freedom. 2009: National Medal of Arts.
2015: Kennedy Center Honors. 2019: Peabody Career Achievement Award.
2021: Appeared in the West Side Story remake.

people.name: Julia de Burgos
body: On July 6, 1953, a woman collapsed on a street in Harlem. By EBSCO's account, she died at Harlem Hospital without anyone knowing who she was and was buried in New York's Potter's Field. About a month later she was identified, and her family brought her body home to Carolina, Puerto Rico. She was Julia de Burgos, now seen as one of the most important poets Puerto Rico has produced.

She was born Julia Constanza Burgos García on February 17, 1914, in a rural part of Carolina, the oldest of thirteen children. Six of her siblings died in childhood, and EBSCO reports malnutrition as the cause. She won a scholarship to the University of Puerto Rico in 1931, graduated in 1933 with a teaching credential, and taught in the rural community of Cedro Arriba in Naranjito.

The 1930s were a time of intense debate over Puerto Rico's status. De Burgos joined the Nationalist Party in 1936 and urged women to support independence. In 1938 she published her first poetry collection, Poema en veinte surcos, and in 1939 her Canción de la verdad sencilla won a poetry prize.

In 1940 she left for New York and later that year went to Cuba with her partner, the Dominican Dr. Juan Isidro Jimenes Grullón, staying about two years. EBSCO reports that she returned to New York in 1942 after his family rejected her because of her African heritage. In 1943 she became a columnist for the New York Spanish-language paper Pueblos Hispanos. Her later years were marked by illness, including alcoholism. El mar y tú appeared after her death, in 1954.

Her reputation grew after her death. Composers set her poems to music, and parks, streets and schools in Puerto Rico bear her name. Poets.org calls her a forerunner of the Nuyorican literary movement of Puerto Rican writers in New York. In 1995 Northwestern University Press published Song of the Simple Truth, her complete poems in English and Spanish, and in 2010 the U.S. Postal Service honored her with a stamp.
keyFacts: 1914: Born February 17 in Carolina, Puerto Rico.
1933: Graduated from the University of Puerto Rico.
1936: Joined the Nationalist Party.
1938: Poema en veinte surcos. 1939: Canción de la verdad sencilla.
1940: Moved to New York; columnist for Pueblos Hispanos from 1943.
1953: Died in Harlem, at 39.
1995: Complete poems published in English and Spanish.

people.name: Pedro del Valle
body: In the spring of 1945, Major General Pedro del Valle commanded the 1st Marine Division in the Battle of Okinawa, and EBSCO credits him with directing the capture of Shuri Castle. His Navy Distinguished Service Medal citation calls him "a brilliant tactician." He was born in San Juan, Puerto Rico.

Del Valle was born on August 28, 1893. His father, Francisco del Valle, was a physician and a former mayor of San Juan. Puerto Rico was then a Spanish colony, and it passed to the United States after the war of 1898. In 1900 the family moved to Maryland. A Puerto Rican governor's appointment brought him to the U.S. Naval Academy, and in 1915 he graduated and was commissioned in the Marine Corps.

His early career followed U.S. interventions in the Caribbean and Central America. He served in Santo Domingo in 1916, then in Haiti and in Nicaragua against the forces of Augusto Sandino. In World War I he commanded the Marine detachment on the USS Texas. Between the wars he helped develop Marine amphibious doctrine. He served as assistant naval attaché in Rome and observed Italy's war in Ethiopia, which he described in the book Roman Eagle over Ethiopia (1940).

In March 1941 he took command of the 11th Marines, an artillery regiment, and led it on Guadalcanal. He was promoted to brigadier general on October 1, 1942. In 1944 he led corps artillery on Guam. EBSCO identifies him as the first Latino to reach major general in the Marine Corps. He retired as a lieutenant general, and the Marine Corps' 2019 Hispanic Heritage Month message says he is acknowledged as the first Hispanic Marine Corps lieutenant general.
After the war he was the Marine Corps inspector general. He retired in January 1948 and later worked for International Telephone and Telegraph. He died on April 28, 1978.
keyFacts: 1893: Born August 28 in San Juan, Puerto Rico; family moved to Maryland in 1900.
1915: Graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy and commissioned in the Marine Corps.
1942: Promoted to brigadier general on October 1, during the Guadalcanal campaign.
1945: Commanded the 1st Marine Division on Okinawa; Navy Distinguished Service Medal.
Acknowledged by the Marine Corps as the first Hispanic Marine Corps lieutenant general.
1948: Retired in January. 1978: Died April 28.

people.name: Olga D. González-Sanabria
body: Batteries that can be charged and drained thousands of times without wearing out are essential to spacecraft, which pass in and out of sunlight. In 1988 a group of NASA researchers that included Olga González-Sanabria received an R&D 100 Award for long cycle-life nickel-hydrogen batteries. Ada Lovelace Day reports that this kind of battery has been used on the International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope and Mars Odyssey.

González-Sanabria grew up in Patillas, on Puerto Rico's southeast coast. She earned a bachelor's degree in chemical engineering from the University of Puerto Rico in 1978. In 1979 she joined NASA's Lewis Research Center (now Glenn Research Center) in Cleveland, Ohio, researching energy storage for space, and in 1985 she earned a master's degree from the University of Toledo.

Her research focused on nickel-hydrogen batteries, especially battery separators. She contributed to more than 30 technical papers and is a co-patentee on a separator technology for alkaline batteries.

She then moved into leadership. She became the center's executive officer in 1995 and led its Plans and Programs Office from 1998 to 2002. NASA describes her as the center's first Latina in the federal Senior Executive Service, and its biography gives both 1995 and 2002 for that step. She became director of Engineering and Technical Services in 2004 and director of the Engineering Directorate in 2008. She retired in December 2011 after 32 years with NASA.

Her honors include NASA's Exceptional Service Medal (1993) and Outstanding Leadership Medal (2002), induction into the Ohio Women's Hall of Fame (2003) and the Presidential Rank of Meritorious Executive (2007). In 2021 she was inducted into the NASA Glenn Research Center Hall of Fame.
keyFacts: Grew up in Patillas, Puerto Rico.
1978: B.S. in chemical engineering, University of Puerto Rico.
1979: Joined NASA Lewis (now Glenn) Research Center.
1988: R&D 100 Award, with her group, for long cycle-life nickel-hydrogen batteries.
2008: Director of Glenn's Engineering Directorate.
2011: Retired in December.
2021: Inducted into the NASA Glenn Hall of Fame.

people.name: Orlando Cepeda
body: On April 15, 1958, the San Francisco Giants played the first major-league game ever held in California. A 20-year-old first baseman from Puerto Rico played that day and hit his first big-league home run. Orlando Cepeda went on to be the unanimous National League Rookie of the Year that season. Before reaching San Francisco, he had played minor-league ball in Minnesota.

Cepeda was born on September 17, 1937, in Ponce. His father, Pedro "Perucho" Cepeda, was a star shortstop in Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic. The son, nicknamed "The Baby Bull," signed with the New York Giants after a tryout camp. He worked his way up through minor-league teams that included the St. Cloud Rox in 1956, when he won the Northern League Triple Crown, and the Giants' Triple-A team in Minneapolis in 1957.

In the majors he played for the Giants, St. Louis Cardinals, Atlanta Braves, Oakland Athletics, Boston Red Sox and Kansas City Royals, ending in 1974. In 1967 he was the unanimous National League Most Valuable Player for the Cardinals, hitting .325 and leading the league with 111 runs batted in. Over his career he collected 2,351 hits and 379 home runs, with a .297 batting average.

His life after baseball had a hard chapter. He was arrested in December 1975 for taking delivery of marijuana, was convicted in 1978 and served ten months in a minimum-security prison. He rebuilt his public life, and for more than 25 years he served as a community ambassador for the Giants. He was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame on July 25, 1999, and the Giants unveiled a statue of him in 2008. He died on June 28, 2024, in Concord, California.
keyFacts: 1937: Born September 17 in Ponce, Puerto Rico.
1956: Northern League Triple Crown with the St. Cloud Rox.
1957: Played for the Giants' Triple-A team in Minneapolis.
1958: Unanimous National League Rookie of the Year.
1967: Unanimous National League MVP.
1999: Inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
2024: Died June 28.
people.connectToWork: How does your work treat someone with a past conviction who has rebuilt their life? Which of your rules look only backward?

people.name: Jesús Colón
body: In 1961 a small New York publisher released A Puerto Rican in New York and Other Sketches, a collection of short pieces about working-class Puerto Rican life in the city. It is considered one of the first books in English by a Puerto Rican author about the Puerto Rican experience. Its author, Jesús Colón, had spent more than four decades writing for newspapers and organizing workers.

Colón was born on January 20, 1901, in Cayey, Puerto Rico, into a poor rural family. As a student he joined the newly formed Socialist Party in San Juan. In 1917, at about sixteen, he moved to New York to live with his older brother, and he worked in factories and as a dockworker, dishwasher, waiter and postal clerk.

In 1918 he helped found the first Puerto Rican committee of the Socialist Party in New York. He took part in early community groups such as Alianza Obrera Puertorriqueña and La Liga Puertorriqueña e Hispana. He led the Cervantes Fraternal Society, part of the International Workers Order, a mutual-aid and insurance group for workers, which was shut down in 1954 after Red Scare investigations.

Throughout, Colón wrote, in Spanish-language papers in New York and in Justicia, a socialist paper in Puerto Rico, sometimes under pen names. From 1955 he wrote a column for the Communist Party's Daily Worker and later the Daily World, where many of the sketches in his 1961 book first appeared. He ran for office on the American Labor Party line, and in 1969 he ran for New York City comptroller on the Communist Party ticket.

He died on May 14, 1974. His papers are held at the Center for Puerto Rican Studies at Hunter College. In 1993 Arte Público Press published The Way It Was, and Other Writings, edited by Edna Acosta-Belén and Virginia Sánchez Korrol.
keyFacts: 1901: Born January 20 in Cayey, Puerto Rico.
1917: Moved to New York.
1918: Helped found the first Puerto Rican committee of the Socialist Party in New York.
1955: Began a column for the Daily Worker, later the Daily World.
1961: Published A Puerto Rican in New York and Other Sketches.
1974: Died May 14.

people.name: Germán Parodi
body: In September 2017, Germán Parodi was protesting for disability rights in Washington, D.C., when he learned Hurricane María was heading for Puerto Rico, where he was born and raised. Soon after the storm, he helped lead a three-week deployment of disabled first responders. The team worked with the island disability organization MAVI and with FEMA, and Next City reports that it supported more than 100 families in the mountainous areas of the island.

Parodi uses a wheelchair. By the organization's account he acquired a spinal cord injury in 2001, moved to Philadelphia in 2004, and was welcomed into the independent living movement there by Philly ADAPT and Liberty Resources. He has co-directed The Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies with Shaylin Sluzalis since September 2019, when it became an independent nonprofit.

During Hurricane Ian in 2022, his team helped people who had been discharged from hospitals too early get into hotel rooms with attendant care. He has called the electric grid "the primary problem of recovering Puerto Rico." He told Stanford Social Innovation Review, "Oftentimes, emergency managers only see us as patients instead of collaborators."
keyFacts: Born and raised in Puerto Rico.
2017: Helped lead a disabled first-responder deployment after Hurricane María.
Since 2019: Co-executive director of The Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies.

people.name: Gretchelle Dilán
body: More than three months after Hurricane María, Gretchelle Dilán still had to drive over an hour from home to get stable cell reception, and her power had been out for over 90 days. She told United Spinal Association about people "forced to just lie in their houses, developing pressure sores," and that "we had to share our catheters amongst each other."

Dilán is a psychologist from Puerto Rico with a doctorate and a wheelchair user, paralyzed by a stray bullet in 2012. She founded Vivo Sin Barreras (Living Without Barriers) for people with disabilities, caregivers and families, and later affiliated it with United Spinal as its Puerto Rico chapter. She launched La Voz Corre, a quarterly Spanish-language magazine for the disability community, and ran an equipment recycling program that collected donated beds and wheelchairs in her garage.

After the storm, United Spinal supplied the chapter with power inverters that run from car batteries. Her advice was practical: "manual chairs are a must," even for people who do not normally use them, because "you can't know how long you'll be without power." The most recent accounts of her work we could find are United Spinal's from 2016 and early 2018.
keyFacts: Founder of United Spinal's Puerto Rico chapter.
Doctorate in psychology; paralyzed in 2012.
Founded Vivo Sin Barreras and the magazine La Voz Corre.

institutions.name: El Museo del Barrio
institutions.location: 1230 Fifth Avenue, East Harlem, New York City
body: In 1969 Raphael Montañez Ortiz, a Puerto Rican artist and teacher, founded a museum in East Harlem, known as El Barrio, working with Puerto Rican educators, artists and community activists. Latino Rebels reports that African American and Puerto Rican parents, teachers and activists in Central and East Harlem wanted an education that addressed their children's backgrounds and cultures, and that Ortiz pressed the local school district to meet those needs. The founders saw that mainstream museums largely ignored Latino artists.

The museum began in a public school. From 1969 to 1976 it occupied a brownstone with several storefronts, and it later found a permanent home on Fifth Avenue at 104th Street. It offers bilingual public programs, education and festivals for neighborhood residents. Its focus has since broadened from Puerto Rican and Caribbean art to Latino culture more widely, and its collection now spans Latinx, Caribbean and Indigenous art.
keyFacts: 1969: Founded by Raphael Montañez Ortiz with Puerto Rican educators, artists and community activists.
Began in a public school; occupied a brownstone from 1969 to 1976.
Now at 1230 Fifth Avenue, at 104th Street.
Offers bilingual programs, education and festivals.
institutions.connectToWork: When people built their own institution because yours left them out, what does that tell you about yours? Who could you learn from without asking them to fix it?

institutions.name: Center for Puerto Rican Studies (CENTRO), Hunter College
institutions.location: Hunter College, City University of New York, 2180 Third Avenue, East Harlem, New York City
body: A coalition of students, faculty and activists founded the center at Hunter College in 1973, wanting to bring the community into the university and carry the university's work out into the community.

Its early research task forces produced books on Puerto Rican labor migration, including Labor Migration Under Capitalism (1979) and Industry and Idleness (1986), and the film Plena is Work, Plena is Song (1989). In 1987 it founded CENTRO Journal, a peer-reviewed journal in Puerto Rican studies, and in 2013 it launched CENTRO Press.

Its library and archives on Puerto Rican history and life in the diaspora serve researchers, students, teachers, filmmakers, genealogists and the public. The collections include the papers of Jesús Colón.
keyFacts: 1973: Founded at Hunter College by students, faculty and activists.
1979 and 1986: Published Labor Migration Under Capitalism and Industry and Idleness.
1987: Founded CENTRO Journal. 2013: Launched CENTRO Press.
Library and archives at 2180 Third Avenue, New York.

institutions.name: 65th Infantry Regiment, "the Borinqueneers"
institutions.type: U.S. Army regiment, now part of the Puerto Rico National Guard
body: In 1899, one year after the United States took Puerto Rico from Spain, Congress authorized a volunteer military unit on the island. In 1917 it was sent to the Panama Canal Zone, where segregation policy largely kept it out of combat. It became the 65th Infantry Regiment in 1920, and the law that later honored it calls it the last segregated unit composed primarily of Hispanic soldiers.

The regiment's defining service came in Korea. It arrived in 1950, still segregated, and was attached to the 3rd Infantry Division. Its soldiers took the name Borinqueneers, from a Taíno word for Puerto Rico. The regiment helped cover the 1st Marine Division's withdrawal from the Chosin Reservoir and helped secure the evacuation at Hungnam. About 61,000 Puerto Ricans served in the Army during the Korean War, most of them in the 65th. Its soldiers earned 9 Distinguished Service Crosses, about 250 Silver Stars and more than 2,700 Purple Hearts, and Puerto Rican soldiers in Korea suffered more than 740 deaths.

The history also includes a mass court-martial. In December 1952, after soldiers refused orders to retake the Jackson Heights outpost, the Army convicted 91 of desertion and disobeying orders and sentenced them to one to 16 years at hard labor. After the cases became public, Secretary of the Army Robert Stevens pardoned them, overturned the sentences and reinstated them. History.com reports that a later internal investigation blamed poor leadership, an ammunition shortage, flawed tactics and ethnic prejudice.

The regiment was fully integrated by 1953. It left the regular Army in 1956 and in 1959 became the only regular Army unit ever transferred to the National Guard. On June 10, 2014, President Barack Obama signed a law awarding the Borinqueneers the Congressional Gold Medal, formally presented in April 2016.
keyFacts: 1899: Congress authorized a volunteer unit in Puerto Rico; redesignated the 65th Infantry Regiment in 1920.
1950: Arrived in Korea as a segregated unit; fully integrated by 1953.
About 61,000 Puerto Ricans served in the Army during the Korean War; more than 740 were killed.
1952: 91 soldiers convicted by court-martial; later pardoned.
1959: Only regular Army unit ever transferred to the National Guard.
2014: Public Law 113-120 awarded the Congressional Gold Medal.
institutions.connectToWork: When you ask an older adult about their life, does your process leave room for military service? How would you ask, and let them decide what to share?

institutions.name: Movimiento para el Alcance de Vida Independiente (MAVI)
body: MAVI was created on June 28, 1988, by community members with disabilities, who set up Puerto Rico's first independent living center under a board led by people with disabilities. By its own account it now has five offices and a mobile unit, and it serves people with disabilities in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Services include independent living skills training, peer counseling, supported employment and benefits planning for Social Security beneficiaries. NBC News called it one of the largest groups representing people with disabilities in Puerto Rico. After Hurricane María, MAVI and the government's disability rights agency visited shelters and contacted mayors to find disabled survivors. NBC reported in 2018 that MAVI did not get access to federally funded emergency equipment such as generators until the following April.
keyFacts: 1988: Founded June 28 as Puerto Rico's first independent living center.
Five offices and a mobile unit, by its own account.
Runs benefits planning for Social Security beneficiaries.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Puerto Rican means people connected to Puerto Rico by birth or family, on the island or the mainland, who differ widely in generation, race, income, language and faith. People born in Puerto Rico are U.S. citizens, so immigration status is generally not the barrier here that it can be for other Latino groups. We did not find a Minnesota study of how Puerto Rican Minnesotans understand disability. The research below is small, mostly older, and sometimes groups Puerto Rican families with others, and for several studies we could read only the abstract.
questions: What do you think explains what's going on for you or your child? What has the school or doctor told you?
Has anyone given you or your child a label? Do you agree with it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Which language do you prefer for reading documents, and which for talking? Would you like an interpreter?
Did you get services in Puerto Rico? What worked and what didn't?
Who helped you most back home, and who helps you here?
Is faith or a faith community part of how your family gets support? Would you like it included in planning?
Has a hurricane, earthquake or power outage affected you or your equipment? What would you want a backup plan to cover?
What words do you use for your disability or your child's, in English and in Spanish?

context.heading: Who is counted in Minnesota
body: Minnesota Compass estimates 22,925 Puerto Rican residents (plus or minus 2,722), using American Community Survey data for 2020 to 2024. About 13.3 percent (plus or minus 3.4) have a disability, by the survey's questions. Those questions do not catch everyone who may identify as disabled, and a group this size has wide margins of error, so this figure does not describe any community or person.
About 38 percent of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home, and about 10.7 percent speak English less than "very well." Do not assume Spanish-only or English-only.

sources.label: Minnesota Compass, Puerto Rican population

context.heading: When a family does not accept a school label
body: In an ethnographic study published in 1992, Beth Harry worked with 12 low-income parents of Puerto Rican heritage whose children had been classified by their schools with a learning disability or mild intellectual disability, using the terms of that time. She found that "different cultural meanings of disability and normalcy led parents to reject the notion of disability." The parents pointed to family identity, language confusion and harmful school practices, not to a problem inside the child.

It is a small, old study and describes no one today. It is a reason not to read disagreement with a label as denial: it may be a reasoned explanation, including concern about English-only instruction. Record both views.

sources.label: Harry, Exceptional Children (1992), abstract

context.heading: Faith and family support
body: A 2001 study of 250 Mexican-origin and Puerto Rican parents of young children with developmental delays, in the United States, found that most described themselves as religious and used religious frameworks to make sense of their child's disability. Parents found their personal faith more supportive than their church, and support shifted after they learned of the condition. The abstract does not separate Puerto Rican results. The study does not show that faith replaced services. Ask, and include a faith community only if the person wants it.

A 1999 study compared 55 Puerto Rican mothers of young children with disabilities in Puerto Rico with 39 in Florida. Family needs were similar, but mothers on the island reported significantly more sources of support. One possible reading is that a move can shrink a support network. That is worth asking about, not assuming. The research we found does not document particular gender or elder roles, so ask who takes part in decisions and caregiving, and hear the person directly.

sources.label: Skinner, Correa, Skinner and Bailey, American Journal on Mental Retardation (2001), abstract
Reyes-Blanes, Correa and Bailey, Topics in Early Childhood Special Education (1999), abstract

context.heading: Autism and scarce services on the island
body: Anderson-Chavarria's 2021 dissertation at Michigan State University drew on interviews with 35 parents of autistic children and 32 providers in Puerto Rico, with observation from 2017 to 2019. Topics included how families understand autism, theories of cause and vaccination decisions, language, and scarce services. The author argues that these experiences are shaped by history, economics and structure, not only by culture. Check system explanations before reading a choice as cultural.

sources.label: Anderson-Chavarria, Forgotten Families of the Sea and the Sun, Michigan State University (2021)

context.heading: Benefits and disasters
body: NBC News reported in 2018 that Puerto Rico does not have the federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program. Its Aid to the Aged, Blind, or Disabled program paid some people as little as $64 a month, against about $733 for SSI in the 50 states. The article cites a Cornell estimate that more than 21 percent of Puerto Rico's population has a disability, higher than any U.S. state. Someone who has moved from the island may be applying for SSI for the first time. Check current rules, because these figures are from 2018.

NBC also reported that after Hurricane María in 2017, disability organizations waited months for information on survivors and for emergency equipment. Some people who moved after a disaster may carry trauma or distrust from it, and others will not. Include emergency planning and backup power for anyone who depends on electric equipment.

sources.label: NBC News, "Hurricane María exposed big gaps in help for Puerto Rico's disabled" (2018)

context.heading: Words and who is missing
body: In Puerto Rico, impedimentos appears in official use, as in the government agency Defensoría de las Personas con Impedimentos. Follow each person's own words. We found no research on stigmatizing terms specific to Puerto Rican communities, and no Puerto Rican data on stigma, so none is offered here.

Germán Parodi and Gretchelle Dilán, profiled on this page, and MAVI show disabled Puerto Ricans leading disaster response and peer support themselves. We did not find a Minnesota organization serving Puerto Rican disabled people, though the search was limited. Do not treat any one person or organization as speaking for everyone.

organizations.intro: Minnesota Compass estimates 22,925 Puerto Rican residents (plus or minus 2,722; American Community Survey, 2020 to 2024), about two-thirds of them in the Twin Cities. The Minnesota Historical Society calls Puerto Ricans the state's second-largest Latino community. Organized groups we could document are small and center on culture, especially bomba and plena, and on Puerto Rico's status. In 2017, for example, the Puerto Ricans In Minnesota Committee hosted Oscar López Rivera in St. Paul. We could not find current activity for that group. We found no Puerto Rican-specific newspaper in Minnesota, so most outlets below serve Latino audiences broadly. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: BORIKEN Cultural Center
entries.location: St. Paul, with events around the metro (the Minnesota State Arts Board’s 2026 grant list places it in Mounds View, and AMPERS describes it as based on St. Paul’s West Side)
entries.purpose: GiveMN gives 2019 as its founding year; a 2022 University of Minnesota StoryMap says the center was originally El Arco Iris Center for the Arts, established in 1993. Teaches Afro-Puerto Rican music (bomba and plena), Taíno arts, crafts and sports to Minnesota families, and runs youth programs and a Parranda Boricua holiday celebration. Its Boriken Performing Group performs at schools, libraries and festivals. Also posts on Facebook as borikenmn.

entries.name: Minnesota Council on Latino Affairs
entries.purpose: Advises the Governor and Legislature on issues affecting Latino Minnesotans, including Puerto Ricans. Publishes legislative agendas and keeps resource directories. Its site has held a page for Puerto Rican families who relocated after Hurricane María, written by board member Francisco González.

entries.name: Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio
entries.location: St. Paul, 797 East 7th Street, with sites in Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin
entries.purpose: Founded in 1981 and calls itself Minnesota's largest Latino-led nonprofit. Programs include behavioral health, career training, early childhood, and Latino elder programs. Serves Latino groups broadly; not specific to Puerto Ricans.

entries.name: Centro Tyrone Guzman
entries.purpose: Founded in 1974 as Centro Cultural Chicano and renamed in 2014. Runs early childhood, youth, elder and respite programs for Latino families. Not specific to Puerto Ricans.

entries.name: Latino Chamber of Commerce of Minnesota
entries.purpose: Supports Latino entrepreneurs through networking and advocacy, and keeps a business directory and job board.

entries.name: Minnesota Historical Society
entries.purpose: Its podcast Minnesota Unraveled has covered how music keeps Puerto Rican Minnesotans connected to their heritage, and it announced the Pedacito de Tierra concert for January 2026. Its programs are occasional, not a Puerto Rican service.

entries.purpose: Latin entertainment and community news, distributed at Hispanic businesses.

entries.purpose: Daily news on health, immigration, politics, sports and business for Latino Minnesotans.

entries.name: LatinoJustice PRLDEF
aliases: Puerto Rican Legal Defense and Education Fund
entries.location: New York, with regional offices in Orlando and Austin
entries.purpose: Founded in 1972 as the Puerto Rican Legal Defense and Education Fund. Its early cases established bilingual education rights for New York City students and enforced bilingual ballots and interpreters for Puerto Rican voters.
